title: The diamond's name (section 13)
hookLine: the sutra is named the diamond that cuts; the thirty-two marks are no marks

cards: Partway through the conversation, Subhuti asks an editor's question. What is this teaching called, and how should we keep it? It's a little like naming a child after years of getting to know her.
The Buddha gives the sutra a name and tells Subhuti to keep it by that name. Then, almost in the next breath, he does to the name what this sutra has been doing to everything else.

teach.b: First, the question: what should this teaching be called, and how should it be kept?
Second, the name, and then the cut. It's called the Diamond Perfection of Wisdom, the Buddha says, and by that name it should be kept.
The Sanskrit title begins with vajra, a word that can mean diamond or thunderbolt, and the full title goes into English in more than one way: the diamond-cutter, the diamond that cuts.

Some readers hear a diamond, which cuts everything and is cut by nothing. Others hear the thunderbolt. Then the cut: what the Buddha calls the perfection of wisdom, he says, is not the perfection of wisdom.
The name is given, and at once kept from hardening. Third, dust and worlds. Is the fine dust in all the worlds a lot?
That dust, the Buddha says, is not dust; that's why it's called dust. The world is not a world; that's why it's called a world. Fourth, the marks again.
Can the Tathagata be seen by the thirty-two marks? No, Subhuti says.

teach.h: THE THIRTY-TWO MARKS ARE NO MARKS.
teach.b: The thirty-two marks are no marks; that's why they're called the thirty-two marks. Section five asked about marks; here they return, with their number. The sutra doesn't stop using words.
It says dust, world, wisdom, marks.
What it cuts is the grip on them. People carry names like that too: the reliable one, the difficult one, the quiet one. A name like that can be used without being held like a fist.

how: In Mahayana communities the sutra is known by its short name, the Diamond Sutra, and is chanted and copied under that name.

o: the sutra is named, then the name is cut so it can't harden
the name of the diamond the Buddha wore on his robe
a jeweler's word for a gem cut to perfect shape

p: is not the perfection of wisdom
is not dust, so it's called dust

s: the Buddha gives the sutra a name, then says the name isn't it
the perfection of wisdom, he says, is not the perfection of wisdom; that's why it's called so.
vajra in the title can only mean diamond
it can mean diamond or thunderbolt, and readers hear it both ways.
section thirteen says dust and worlds don't exist
it says dust is not dust, so it's called dust. the words are used, not grasped.

games.q: you're Subhuti, and you've just asked what to call this teaching. the Buddha gives it a name. what does he do next?
o: tells you never to say the name aloud.
says the perfection of wisdom is not the perfection of wisdom.
lists the other names it should never be called.
games.why: he cuts the name in the same breath: what's called the perfection of wisdom is not the perfection of wisdom, and that's why it's called so.

practice: Let your eyes rest on one object near you, a cup, a lamp, your own hand, and say its name once inside: cup. Keep looking and let the name go quiet, noticing what's still there, color, shine, a chip in the rim, the light on it.
Then say the name once more, lightly, as a tool and not a cage, and go back and forth as slowly as you like.

wordCard.voice: The diamond's name. The sutra is called the Diamond Perfection of Wisdom, and then the name itself is cut: the perfection of wisdom is not the perfection of wisdom. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: diamond or thunderbolt; the first word of the sutra's Sanskrit title.

carryVoice: Your line: the diamond cuts. A name can be a tool and not a cage. See you at section fourteen.
